extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: practising geologists, sedimentologists, physicists, marine/civil engineers, and natural historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on methods and observational criteria used in 19th-century natural-science notes for identifying the source of sand/sandstone and related physical/geological observations. Emphasises polarised-light microscopy and allied observational standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarised-light discrimination of quartz vs flint in sand grains
rubrics_metrics.description: Polarised light differentiates sand produced by breaking-up of quartz from sand produced by breaking-up of flint in a decisive way that ordinary light microscopy and chemical analysis do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quartz grains appear resplendent with prismatic colours under polarized light; flint shows a cold steel-grey surface covered with a peculiar marking (described as a species of reticulation). Once seen, the marking is easily recognised. Some cherts (e.g., Portlandian) show the same marking as flint. This method therefore provides a reliable diagnostic for distinguishing quartz-derived vs flint-derived sand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarised-light identification of chalcedony (crystallinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polarised light shows chalcedony to be, like quartz, a crystalline instead of a non-crystalline substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under polarised light chalcedony bears the same relation to quartz crystals and massive quartz as fibrous gypsum does to selenite and common gypsum; this observation corrects the usual teaching that chalcedony is non-crystalline and can be used as a diagnostic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field criteria distinguishing dolmens from chambered tumuli (barrow kists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dolmens and the barrow kists (chambered tumuli) can be distinguished by on-site structural and contextual features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed differences include: (1) Dolmens in Finistére are invariably bare while kists are constantly covered—no signs of degradation on kists and no sign of former covering on dolmens; (2) Chambered tumuli almost always possess a floor-stone at the base, whereas the dolmens examined lack such floor-stones (and floor-stones would be the last to be removed if mounds eroded); (3) Dolmens were generally erected without careful adjustment of sides or tops, while many entombed kists show tokens of care and trouble in their construction. Therefore it is premature to assume dolmens are merely the skeletons of original chambered tumuli; apply these structural checks (presence of floor-stone, evidence of original covering, workmanship) when comparing the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave-height prediction by exposure-distance (square-root law) and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: For many observations the height of waves increases most nearly in the ratio of the square root of their distances from the windward shore (crest describes a parabolic curve): if h = wave height, d = distance of exposure, and a is a coefficient depending on wind strength, then h = a * sqrt(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For heavy gales a may be taken about 1.5 for practical engineering; alternate formulae are provided for short distances (under ~10 miles). Caveats: the height reaching a particular work may be reduced by shallowing (waves breaking before the work), so the maximum height possible in a given depth requires separate determination. Empirical observations at Scarborough (1870) showed waves breaking when water depth below trough was about twice their own height, contradicting the practical limits asserted by Mr. Scott Russell (who said certain maxima had not been observed). Also, larger waves are not always most destructive because they may break on outlying rocks or bars—smaller waves may cause greater harbour range. Use the square-root relation as an empirical starting point but account for local depth, bars, and breaking behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical measurement method for wave breaking at structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure wave heights and breaking depths at fixed pier features (iron piles, slip gratings) to determine the depths at which waves of given classes break and compare with theoretical limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Scarborough the author measured heights from hollow to crest and recorded mean depths of water below trough; use these observations to test theoretical laws (e.g., Russell's maxima). Record both mean and highest wave heights, note whether depths are measured below trough or still-water level, and relate observations to local bathymetry and presence of bars/outlying rocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory design and apparatus arrangement standards for a university physical laboratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical design features and conventions that facilitate teaching and experimental work in a university physical laboratory and lecture-room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended features (as implemented at Glasgow University) include: a large lecture-room with a glass-covered turret above lecture table and darkness-able windows (double blue baize curtains); ventilation per Phipson's plan with fresh air shafts and powered fans; benches arranged for ~150 students rising at ~25°; provision under benches for battery cells; laboratory below lecture-room with isolated masonry piers for steady tables (tables rest on piers without floor contact to avoid vibration transfer); separate apparatus and store rooms; permanent gas-holders (oxygen and hydrogen) for ready oxyhydrogen light; heavy, insulated electrode runs for powerful batteries; pillars for very steady instrument supports; suspension design and perfect symmetry for long Foucault pendulum (to demonstrate earth rotation); clock-control by telegraphic currents for time-keeping. These design choices increase steadiness, reliability, and convenience of demonstrations and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemic-analysis approach using mapped foci and periodic celestial correlations (cholera hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed method for analysing cholera outbreaks by identifying multiple geographic 'homes' (foci) and treating epidemics as propagating atmospheric 'streams', then seeking correlations with solar/auroral/planetary periodicities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author proposes seven 'homes' near the Tropic of Cancer producing atmospheric streams (~1,400 miles wide) whose northwest and southwest advances account for recorded cholera spread; observed synchronous dual advances imply geometric relations on maps. He also claims a parallelism between cholera epidemic maxima/minima and sunspot cycles (periods and subperiods), suggesting cosmic/solar influences (auroral displays, magnetic and earth-current periodicities) may be connected to cholera periodicity. Use careful mapping of outbreak progress, compare timing with solar/auroral/planetary cycles, and consider environmental correlates (east winds, river deltas, tertiary/alluvial strata) when analysing cholera spread. The author notes this is a hypothesis to be tested and not definitive proof of causation.
